questions.q: What does `set -e` change about how a script runs?
options: It suppresses all error messages
The script exits immediately if any command returns a nonzero exit status
It automatically retries a failed command
It makes every variable local by default
questions.explain: Without set -e, Bash continues running a script even after a command fails. set -e stops execution immediately at the first failing command.

questions.q: With `set -u` enabled, what happens when the script references `$enviroment` (a typo for `$environment`)?
options: It silently expands to an empty string, same as without set -u
The script errors out with 'unbound variable' instead of silently continuing with an empty value
Bash automatically corrects the typo
set -u has no effect on unset variables
questions.explain: set -u treats referencing an unset variable as an error, which catches typos that would otherwise silently evaluate to an empty string.

questions.q: In `grep "ERROR" missing.log | wc -l`, why might the pipeline report success even though grep failed?
options: Pipelines always report success regardless of any command's result
Without pipefail, a pipeline's exit status reflects only the last command (wc -l), which can succeed even if an earlier command failed
grep never returns a nonzero exit status
wc -l overrides grep's exit status intentionally as a bug
questions.explain: By default, a pipeline's exit status is that of its last command. set -o pipefail changes this so the pipeline fails if any command in it fails.

It runs the rm command whenever the script exits, whether normally, on error, or when interrupted
It prevents the script from ever exiting
It schedules the deletion to happen the next day via cron
questions.explain: A trap on EXIT runs the given command when the script exits for any reason, which is why it's a reliable way to guarantee cleanup like removing a temp file.

questions.q: What does `bash -x script.sh` do that's useful for debugging?
options: It only checks the script's syntax without running it
It prints each command, with variable substitutions already applied, immediately before executing it
It runs the script faster by skipping comments
It automatically fixes any errors found
questions.explain: The -x flag turns on command tracing, printing each command (after substitution) as it executes, which makes it easy to see exactly what the script is doing step by step.
